3. Respondent Nos. 4 and 5 as well as respondent No. 6 opposed the Rule and filed separate affidavits-in-opposition and the common stand taken by them is that in both the nomination papers there were overwriting on the voter's numbers of the proposer as well as the petitioner/ candidate causing variation of voter numbers from that of the Electoral Roll and so both the nomination papers filed on 23-12-2002 and 31-12-2002 were rejected and that in terms of Rule 11 of the Union Parishad Election Rules 1983, hereinafter referred to as Rules 1983, the petitioner/candidate was disqualified and that he without any basis made wild allegations to the effect that due to political influence the respondent Nos. 4 and 5, by illegal means, got the nomination papers filed by the petitioner rejected. 

 4. Dr M Zahir, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, submits that it is only on four grounds as provided in sub-rule (a)(b)(c) and (d) and (d) of Rule 15(3) of the Rules 1983 that the respondent No.5 could reject the nomination papers filed by the petitioner and that the respondent No. 6 in collusion with the other respondents made the overwriting on the voter numbers of the proposer as well as the petitioner/candidate resulting in variation of the voter number from that of the Electoral Rolls, but such variations in the nomination paper do not come within above sub-rules (a)(b)(c) and (d) of rule 15(3) and further, in terms of section 7(1)(c) of (Union Parishad) Ordinance 1983, hereinafter Ordinance 1983, for the post of chairman of Union Parishad, any candidate whose name appeared on the electoral roll for any ward in the concerned Union was qualified to contest and in the present case the name of the petitioner admittedly appeared on the electoral roll of the concerned ward and so the rejection of the nomination paper on ground of such variation is illegal. Dr Zahir next submits that it is very natural that the petitioner, who earlier was elected chairman consecutively, would not have made such overwriting which resulted in ousting him from the election race and the legal presumption is that the sole beneficiary i.e. the respondent No. 6, who got elected as Chairman uncontested, in collusion with the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 and also other candidates, who later on withdrew their nomination papers so that the proforma respondents No. 6 may get elected uncontested, caused the overwriting in the nomination paper by taking resort to fraud and forgery, while those were under the custody of the respondent No. 5 and then on the plea of variation of voter number got the nomination papers rejected. Further, the declaration of the proforma respondent No. 6 as the uncontested chairman by an antedated order and the publication of the Gazette Notification even after notice of the fact that the High Court Division has granted stay, show the malafide of the respondents. 

 5. Mr Abdus Samad Kamal, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for respondent Nos. 4 and 5, submits that since the proforma respondent No. 6 has already been declared as chairman under rule 20(3) of the Rules 1983, law does not contemplate intervention by this court by invoking jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution during intermediate stage which will undermine the process of election and the smooth running of democratic institutions and the grievance of the petitioner being an "election dispute", the same should be decided exclusively by the Election Tribunal constituted under special statute and the respondent No. 5 lawfully rejected both the nomination papers filed by the petitioner because due to overwriting the voter number of the proposer as shown in the nomination paper dated 23-12-2002 clearly varied from voter number shown in the Electoral Roll and likewise due to similar overwriting the voter number of the petitioner/candidate as shown in the nomination paper filed on 31-12-2002 also varied from number shown in the Electoral Roll and in view of the above, in terms of sub-rules (2) and (3) of rule 11 (2) of Rules 1983 the petitioner is disqualified and the allegations to the effect that the proforma respondent No.6 in collusion with respondent Nos. 4-5 and other candidates, caused the overwriting defects in the nomination papers by fraud and forgery, is totally false and moreover, the errors found in both the nomination papers being of substantial nature, come within the disqualification clause as provided in sub-rules (a)(b)( c) and (d) of Rule 15(3) of the Rules 1983 and so the respondent No. 5 had no other alternative but to reject those nomination papers. 

 9. In the present case in terms of the serial shown in the Electoral Roll, the petitioner/ candidate, who filed the nomination papers for the post of Chairman, is qualified to be a candidate for post of Chairman and similarly, Shah Alam, the proposer, is also qualified to subscribe the name of the petitioner in the nomination paper for the post of Chairman. Further, there is also nothing on record to show that dispute has been raised by any person to the effect that the voter numbers of the petitioner as well as the proposer are wrong and/or signature of the proposer is not genuine. 

 10. from the contents of the provisions of Rule 15 of Rules 1983 as quoted above the Returning Officer at the time of scrutiny under Rule 15 of the Rules 1983 has not given any power to reject the nomination papers filed by the candidate because of variation of voter number of the proposer or the candidate in the nomination paper filed by the candidate for the post of Chairman of Union Parishad. Similarly, in section 7(2) of the Ordinance 1983 there is also no ground to the effect that because of the variation of the voter number of the proposer and/or the candidate as given in nomination papers from that of the Electoral Roll, the candidate will be disqualified. 

 11. However sub-rule (3) of Rule 11 of the Rules 1983 on which the respondents rely, merely provides that every proposal for election of a Chairman shall be made in Form-A, there is a space for putting the voter's number of the candidate for Chairman as well as the proposer and the seconder and accordingly, in Form-A the voter numbers of the candidate, the proposer and also the seconder are given. As mentioned earlier, Ordinance 1983 and Election Rules 1983 contain no provision to the effect that for variation of voter number of the candidate and/or the proposer in Form-A, the Returning Officer may reject the nomination paper. Accordingly, even if for argument's sake, it is conceded that the petitioner himself made the overwriting’s and so voter number of the proposer and/or the candidate as given in Form A, do not tally with that of the Electoral Roll even then, for such defect the Returning Officer cannot reject the nomination paper for the post of Chairman of Union Parishad and rather, in terms of Rule 15(3)(d)(ii), which provides that the Returning Officer shall not reject a nomination paper on the ground of any defect which is not of a substantial nature, the Returning Officer is required to get any such defect to be remedied forthwith and since the Electoral Roll was very much available, the voter numbers of the proposer and petitioner/candidate as shown in the nomination forms ought to have been corrected. In this regard we may take note of the circular No. নিকশ /স্বাঃ নিঃ-১/ইং পঃ/১(১)/২০০২/১৯৫৮(৩৩৬৪)dated 27 -11-2002, the relevant portion of which is quoted specifically provides that even for variation of their nature, the returning officer, instead of rejecting the nomination will take steps of remedying such defects which in the present case could easily be done by comparing with the Electoral Roll. 

 13. Now let us examine whether the erroneous mentioning of the voter numbers of the proposer and/or the petitioner candidate in the nomination paper which varied with the number appearing in the Electoral Roll, is substantial in nature or with malafide motive the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 raised this plea. 

 Between malice in fact and malice in law there is a broad distinction which is not peculiar to any particular system of jurisprudence. A person who inflicts an injury upon another person in contravention of the law is not allowed to say that he did so with an innocent mind; he is taken to know the law, and he must act within the law. He may, therefore, be guilty of malice in law, although so far as the state of his mind is concerned, he acts ignorantly and in that sense innocently, Malice of fact is quite a different thing; it means an actual malicious intention on the part of the person who has done the wrongs independent of contract, a very material ingredient in the question whether a valid cause of action can be stated." 

 "Whenever the statute requires a particular act to be done in a particular manner and also lays down that failure to comply with the said requirement leads to a specific consequence it would be difficult to accept the argument that the failure to comply with the said requirement should lead to any other consequence. There is no doubt that the essential object of the scrutiny of nomination papers is that the returning officer should be satisfied that the candidate who is not an elector in the constituency in question, is in fact, and elector of a different constituency. the satisfaction of the returning officer is thus the matter of substance in these proceedings; section 33(5) requires the candidate to supply the prescribed copy and section 36(2)(b) provides that on his failure to comply with the said requirement his nomination paper is liable to be rejected. In other words, this is a case where the statute requires the candidate to produce the prescribed evidence and provides a penalty for his failure to do so. If the candidate fails to produce the relevant copy, the consequence prescribed by section 36(2)(b) must inevitably follow". 

 Madan Lal, resident of village Parnech, PO Ghananatti, District Mahsau filed two nomination papers before me on 20th January, 1967 which bears serial Nos. 5 and 6. According to the entry in the nomination paper serial no. 5 Shri Anant Ram proposers have been shown to be entered at serial No. 383 of 13 of the electoral rolls for 9-Arki Assembly Constituency. From the comparison with the final copy of electoral rolls for this constituency, at serial No. 383 of part 13 the name of Shrimati Phullu, wife of Shri Nirjal Singh has been entered. As such, this entry in this nomination paper is wrong." 

 "The Returning Officer has the duty to scrutinize the nomination papers when they were presented for finding out whether there were any clerical mistakes in the same. Under that provision he was required to find out whether the names of the candidates as well as their proposers and seconders were correctly mentioned in the nomination papers. He was also required to see whether their place in the electoral roll was correctly mentioned in the nomination papers. Evidently, the Returning Officer failed in his duty. Further, when he scrutinized the nomination papers on January 21, 1967, he has before him all the required information. It may be that while scrutinizing the first nomination paper (marked as No. 5) he has no material before him to find out whether the proposer of the candidate was really an elector in the constituency or not, but when he came to the second nomination paper where the proposer's name as well as his place in the electoral roll is correctly mentioned, it was improper on his part to have rejected that nomination paper. It is true that in that nomination paper, it had been mentioned that the candidate's name is found at serial No. 504 of Part 4 of 9-Arki Assembly Constituency though in fact, it is found at serial No. 504 in Part I; of that constituency; but from the first nomination paper, the Returning Officer could have easily found out the correct part of the electoral roll. All the required information was before him. Obviously he rejected the nomination papers for the reason that the respondent was only a dummy candidate but that was not a matter for him to decide." 

 "The first question that we have got to decide is whether the defects found in the nomination paper of the appellant are of substantial character. As mentioned earlier, the appellant was fully qualified to be nominated for the election. The only thing said against his nomination is that his nomination paper was not properly filled in. We have earlier seen that a duty is imposed on the Returning Officer by sub-section (4) of section 33 to look into the nomination paper when it is presented and to satisfy himself that the names and electoral roll numbers of the candidate and that of the proposer as entered in the nomination paper are the same as those entered in the electoral roll. In this case it is proved that the Returning Officer did look into the nomination paper but unfortunately, he also did not notice that the name of the appellant had been removed from the electoral roll of Arrah constituency. If he had noticed that fact, he would have asked the appellant either to correct the mistake or have earlier noticed that the appellant filed his nomination paper on the 6th of January 1969 and the last date for filing the nomination paper there would have been no difficulty for him either to correct the nomination paper filed or to file a fresh nomination paper. We have earlier noticed that the appellant had with him a certified copy of the electoral roll of the Sandesh Constituency and "he had shown the same to the Returning Officer. Mistakes complained of occurred because both the appellant as well as the Returning Officer merely looked into the main voters list but overlooked the deletion noted in a separate list. But the implication of section 33(4) is that a wrong entry in a nomination paper as regards the name of the candidate or the proposer or their electoral roll numbers is not a matter of substantial importance. That is why the legislature requires the Returning Officer to look into them and if there are any mistake to get it corrected. The requirement in an election is that the candidate should possess all the prescribed qualifications and that he should not have incurred any of the disqualifications mentioned either in the Constitution or in the Act. The other information required to be given in the nomination paper is only to satisfy the Returning Officer that the candidate possesses the prescribed qualification and that he is not otherwise disqualified. In other words that information’s relate to the proof of the required qualifications. " 

 25. Further, within the four corners of section 7 of Ordinance 1983 the candidate is not required to furnish serial number of the electoral roll to be qualified as candidate to contest the election and there is also no provision in law to the effect that non-furnishing or erroneous furnishing of voter number will be a disqualification of the candidate rather in terms of section 7 (1)( c) the appearance of the name of the electoral roll for any ward in the Union is enough for qualifying a candidate to be elected. As discussed earlier, under Rule 15 of the Rules 1983, the Returning Officer at the time of scrutiny has not been empowered to reject the nomination paper if it contained erroneous serial number of the candidate in the electoral roll and he can reject the nomination paper if the defects fall within the four grounds as described in Rule 15(3)(a)(b)(c)(d) of Rules, 1983. In fact, the provision to give the serial number of the voter has been incorporated only in Form A in order to identify the candidate in the electoral role. So, this type of error cannot be considered as substantial in nature as contemplated in the proviso of sub-rule (3) of Rule 15 of the Union Parishad Election Rules, 1983.
